newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Genetic Institute's Neumega.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Genetic Institute's Neumega.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Thursday voted in favor of some uses of Genetic Institute Inc's interleukin-11 (Neumega), a bioengineered hormone that prevents platelet depletion and tranfusion needs due to chemotherapy.

The panel voted to recommend it only for use in patients who have had previous chemotherapy or previous transfusions. Genetics Institute, a unit of American Home Products, wanted to sell Neumega to all patients with solid organ tumors or non-Hodgkins lymphomas who experience thrombocytopenia, or reduced platelet count.
But so far, Neumega only seems to benefit a small group of patients, the panel heard.

The drug has been given orphan drug status by the FDA, which gives Genetics Institute seven years marketing exclusivity, but only for cancer populations under 200,000. That would likely include patients who had previous chemo or transfusions.
The panel voted 14-3 that the data failed to show as big a treatment effect in patients who had not had previous chemotherapy.

That conclusion was based on the second of two studies carried out by the firm. In that randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 68 percent of 40 women getting Neumega avoided transfusion, compared to only 41 percent of placebo patients. The women had advanced breast cancer, and underwent two courses of high-dose cyclophosphamide or doxorubicin. Neumega patients who did need transfusions got an average 0.8, compared to an average 2.2 transfusions in placebo patients. But panelists rejected the results, as there were a number of women who did not complete the study.

The panel considered Genetics Institute's first trial to be stronger. In that study, 38 percent of the 30 patients with solid tumors or lymphomas who got a high dose of Neumega -- 50 micrograms per kilogram -- avoided transfusion, compared to 7 percent of the 30 on placebo. For those who needed transfusions, Neumega patients needed fewer -- 2.2 transfusions on average, compared to 3.4 for placebo.
After assessing all the trial data, FDA reviewer Richard Steffen called Neumega's treatment effect "modest."

The panel also raised some concern about side effects. The most common were swelling and shortness of breath due to fluid retention caused by the drug. More than half of patients reported both effects, according to the FDA. Neumega also "appears to cause cardiac rhythm disturbance," Steffen said. A quarter of patients had tachycardias -- fast heartbeats -- or palpitations and about 15 percent had atrial arrhythmias, or heart fluttering. The fluttering caused several hospitalizations. Despite these side effects, the panel was unanimous that the benefits of Neumega outweigh the risks.
